content: 1. Medications containing aspartame, such as 5 mg and 400 mg/57 mg formulations, should be used with caution. The safety and efficacy of extended-release tablets in children under 16 years of age have not been established. 2. Pexidartinib can cause hepatotoxicity. It is advised to avoid co-administration of pexidartinib with other products known to cause liver toxicity, such as clavulanate and pretomanid, as these combinations may increase toxicity. Alternative drugs should be considered. 3. Pretomanid regimens are associated with hepatotoxicity. Patients should avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic agents, including herbal supplements and drugs other than bedaquiline and linezolid. 4. The combination of mifepristone and clavulanate may increase the risk of elevated liver enzymes. Liver function tests (LFTs) should be closely monitored when these drugs are used together. 5. Valoctocogene roxaparvovec, when combined with medications that may cause hepatotoxicity, can increase the risk of elevated liver enzymes. Close monitoring is required, and alternative medications should be considered to avoid potential drug interactions. 6. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, and hepatotoxicity, have been reported with the use of clavulanate-containing medications. These reactions may include elevated AST/ALT levels, pseudomembranous colitis, and serum sickness. 7. Gastrointestinal side effects such as abdominal discomfort, cholestatic jaundice, flatulence, stomatitis, glossitis, black hairy tongue, mucocutaneous candidiasis, and drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome have been observed. 8. Immune-mediated reactions, including anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions (e.g., shock, angioedema, urticaria, or skin rash accompanied by arthritis, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever), as well as hypersensitivity vasculitis, have been reported. 9. Severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), may occur. If a skin rash develops, patients should be closely monitored, and the drug should be discontinued if lesions progress. 10. Renal side effects, including interstitial nephritis and crystalluria, have been reported. Central nervous system effects, such as agitation, anxiety, behavioral changes, aseptic meningitis, confusion, convulsions, dizziness, insomnia, and reversible hyperactivity, have been rarely observed. 11. Patients with a history of penicillin allergy or previous cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with amoxicillin/clavulanate should avoid this medication. Extended-release tablets are not recommended for patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min) or those undergoing hemodialysis. 12. Different tablet formulations of amoxicillin/clavulanate are not interchangeable due to varying ratios of amoxicillin to clavulanate. The incidence of diarrhea is higher with amoxicillin/clavulanate compared to amoxicillin alone. 13. The safety and efficacy of extended-release tablets in patients under 16 years of age are unknown. There is a risk of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD), which can occur up to two months after antibiotic therapy. If CDAD is suspected, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy, including fluid/electrolyte replacement and C. difficile-specific antibiotics, should be initiated. 14. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. There is also a risk of bacterial or fungal superinfections, which require immediate discontinuation of the drug and appropriate treatment. 15. A high percentage of patients with mononucleosis develop a rash during therapy with ampicillin-class antibiotics, which are not recommended for these patients. 16. Use caution in patients with hepatic impairment, as hepatic dysfunction (though rare) is more common in elderly males and with prolonged therapy. Hepatic dysfunction may occur even after completing therapy. 17. Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. A thorough history of hypersensitivity reactions should be obtained before initiating therapy. If an allergic reaction occurs, treatment should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be instituted. 18. Reproductive studies in animals (mice and rats) at doses up to 10 times the human dose have shown no teratogenic effects. However, a single study in women with preterm premature rupture of the fetal membrane (pPROM) suggested that prophylactic treatment with this drug may increase the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates. Use during pregnancy should be avoided unless deemed essential by the physician. 19. Ampicillin-class antibiotics are excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering the drug to nursing mothers. While trace amounts in breast milk may pose a risk of sensitization, no known detrimental effects have been reported for breastfed infants. 20. The drug is generally considered acceptable during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. 21. Amoxicillin and clavulanic acid are widely distributed in the body (except the CNS), partially metabolized by the liver, and excreted unchanged in the urine. Protein binding is 18% for amoxicillin and 25% for clavulanic acid. 22. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only.
